title: Pinocchio eats the sugar but will not take his medicine; when he sees the gravediggers coming to take him away, he takes it. Then he tells a lie, and his nose grows as punishment.
paragraphs: As soon as the three doctors had left the room, the Fairy went over to Pinocchio and, after touching his forehead, realised that he had a terribly high fever.
Then she dissolved a certain white powder in half a glass of water and, offering it to the puppet, said kindly:
“Drink this, and in a few days you’ll be well.”
Pinocchio looked at the glass, twisted his mouth a little, and then asked in a whining voice:
“Is it sweet or bitter?”
“It’s bitter, but it will do you good.”
“If it’s bitter, I don’t want it.”
“Listen to me: drink it.”
“I don’t like bitter things.”
“Drink it: and when you’ve drunk it, I’ll give you a little ball of sugar to take away the taste.”
“Where’s the sugar ball?”
“Here it is,” said the Fairy, taking it out of a golden sugar bowl.
“I want the sugar ball first, and then I’ll drink that nasty bitter water…”
“Do you promise?”
“Yes…”
The Fairy gave him the sugar ball, and Pinocchio, after crunching it up and swallowing it in an instant, said, licking his lips:
“Wouldn’t it be lovely if sugar were medicine too! I’d take it every day.”
“Now keep your promise and drink these few drops of water, which will make you well.”
Pinocchio reluctantly took the glass and stuck the tip of his nose into it: then he brought it up to his mouth: then he stuck his nose into it again: finally he said:
“It’s too bitter! Too bitter! I can’t drink it.”
“How can you say that when you haven’t even tasted it?”
“I can imagine it! I could tell by the smell. I want another sugar ball first… and then I’ll drink it!”
Then the Fairy, with all the patience of a good mother, put a little more sugar in his mouth; and afterwards she offered him the glass again.
“I can’t drink it like this!” said the puppet, making a thousand faces.
“Why?”
“Because that pillow down there on my feet is bothering me.”
The Fairy took the pillow away.
“It’s no use! I still can’t drink it.”
“What else is bothering you?”
“The bedroom door is bothering me, because it’s half open.”
The Fairy went and closed the bedroom door.
“Anyway,” cried Pinocchio, bursting into tears, “I won’t drink that nasty bitter water, no, no, no!”
“My boy, you’ll regret it…”
“I don’t care…”
“You are very ill.”
“I don’t care…”
“The fever will send you to the other world in a few hours…”
“I don’t care…”
“Aren’t you afraid of death?”
“Not at all! I’d rather die than drink that nasty medicine.”
At this point, the bedroom door flew open and four rabbits as black as ink came in, carrying a little coffin on their shoulders.
“What do you want with me?” cried Pinocchio, sitting up in bed in terror.
“We’ve come to take you away,” replied the largest rabbit.
“Take me away? But I’m not dead yet!”
“Not yet: but you have only a few moments left to live, since you refused to drink the medicine that would have cured your fever!”
“Oh, my Fairy, my Fairy!” the puppet began to scream. “Give me that glass at once… Hurry, please, because I don’t want to die, no… I don’t want to die.”
And taking the glass in both hands, he emptied it in one gulp.
“Oh well!” said the rabbits. “This time we’ve made the trip for nothing.” And lifting the little coffin onto their shoulders again, they left the room grumbling and muttering under their breath.

The fact is that a few minutes later, Pinocchio jumped out of bed, completely well; for you should know that wooden puppets have the special advantage of rarely falling ill and getting better very quickly.
And the Fairy, seeing him running and tumbling around the room, as lively and cheerful as a young cockerel just learning to crow, said:
“So my medicine really did you good?”
“Good? It brought me back to life!”
“Then why did you make me beg you so much to drink it?”
“It’s because we children are all like that! We’re more afraid of medicine than of illness.”
“Shame on you! Children should know that good medicine taken in time can save them from a serious illness and perhaps even from death…”
“Oh! But next time I won’t make you beg so much! I’ll remember those black rabbits with the coffin on their shoulders… and then I’ll take the glass straight away and down it goes…”
“Now come here to me and tell me how you ended up in the murderers’ hands.”

“What happened was that Fire-Eater the puppet-master gave me five gold coins and said, ‘Here, take them to your father!’ and instead I met a Fox and a Cat on the road, two very decent people, who said, ‘Would you like those coins to become a thousand or two thousand? Come with us, and we’ll take you to the Field of Miracles.’ And I said, ‘Let’s go’; and they said, ‘Let’s stop here at the Red Crayfish Inn, and after midnight we’ll set off again.’ And when I woke up, they weren’t there any more because they’d left. Then I started walking in the night, and it was so dark you wouldn’t believe it, so I met two murderers on the road inside coal sacks, and they said, ‘Hand over the money’; and I said, ‘I haven’t got any’; because I’d hidden the gold coins in my mouth, and one of the murderers tried to put his hands in my mouth, and I bit his hand off and then spat it out, but instead of a hand I spat out a cat’s paw. And the murderers chased me, and I ran and ran until they caught up with me, and they tied me by the neck to a tree in this wood, saying, ‘Tomorrow we’ll come back here, and then you’ll be dead with your mouth open, and we’ll take away the gold coins you’ve hidden under your tongue.’”
“And where have you put the four coins now?” the Fairy asked him.
“I’ve lost them!” replied Pinocchio; but he was telling a lie, because they were really in his pocket.
As soon as he told the lie, his nose, which was already long, immediately grew two finger-widths longer.
“And where did you lose them?”
“In the wood nearby.”
At this second lie, his nose kept growing.
“If you lost them in the nearby wood,” said the Fairy, “we’ll look for them and find them: because everything lost in the nearby wood is always found again.”
“Ah! Now I remember properly,” replied the puppet, getting mixed up, “I haven’t lost the four coins, but without noticing, I swallowed them while I was drinking your medicine.”

At this third lie, his nose grew so amazingly long that poor Pinocchio could no longer turn in any direction. If he turned this way, he hit his nose against the bed or the windowpanes, if he turned that way, he hit it against the walls or the bedroom door, if he raised his head a little higher, he risked poking the Fairy in the eye.
And the Fairy looked at him and laughed.
“Why are you laughing?” the puppet asked her, very confused and worried about his nose, which was growing before his eyes.
“I’m laughing at the lie you told.”
“How do you know I told a lie?”
“Lies, my boy, are easy to spot, because there are two kinds: there are lies with short legs, and lies with long noses: yours happens to be one of those with a long nose.”
Pinocchio, not knowing where to hide for shame, tried to run out of the room, but he could not. His nose had grown so long that it would no longer fit through the doorway.
